Between the trees, we've started turning the grass into a wildflower meadow, sown with yellow rattle to weaken the grass, and mown into paths so people can walk through. It'll take a few years to come good. Orchards and meadows both reward patience.

## What happens next

The group now runs pruning workshops each winter and an apple day every October. We still go up a few times a year to see how things are getting on. The first proper crop is perhaps three years away, and we've already been promised a bottle of the perry.

examples.title: Replanting a community orchard in Hebden Bridge
examples.excerpt: Forty-two fruit trees, three planting days, a lot of volunteers and quite a lot of cake. A different kind of project for us, and one of our favourites.
examples.body:
Most of our work is for private gardens. Every so often, though, something different comes along, and this was one of those. A residents' group in Hebden Bridge had taken on a steep, neglected field above the town with a handful of old apple trees in it, and they wanted to turn it back into an orchard everyone could use.

They had enthusiasm, a small grant and a great many volunteers. What they didn't have was a plan. That's where we came in.

## Starting with the old trees

There were eleven old trees on the site, mostly apples, a couple of damsons and one very large perry pear that nobody could identify. We had them looked at by a fruit specialist from the Northern Fruit Group, who confirmed that several were old local varieties worth keeping. Two were too far gone and came down. The rest were given a careful restorative prune, spread over three winters so as not to shock them.

## Choosing what to plant

We added forty-two new trees, chosen for three things: they had to be hardy enough for a cold Pennine hillside, they had to be varieties with some link to the north of England, and they had to fruit over a long season so there was always something to pick.

- Apples including 'Ribston Pippin', 'Keswick Codlin', 'Yorkshire Greening' and 'Lord Lambourne'
- Pears 'Hessle' and 'Catillac', both tough and reliable
- Damsons and plums, including 'Shropshire Prune' and 'Victoria'
- A few cobnuts along the top hedge, for the squirrels if nobody else

All of them are on vigorous rootstocks. On an exposed site, they need the strength, and a community orchard benefits from big trees you can stand under.

## The planting days

We ran three planting days in February, each with around thirty volunteers. We gave a short demonstration at the start, then split everyone into small groups, each with someone who had planted a tree before. By the end of the third day every tree was in, staked and guarded against rabbits and deer.

> Someone's grandchild planted the last tree. That felt right.

## The meadow underneath

Between the trees, we've started turning the grass into a wildflower meadow, sown with yellow rattle to weaken the grass, and mown into paths so people can walk through. It'll take a few years to come good. Orchards and meadows both reward patience.

## What happens next

The group now runs pruning workshops each winter and an apple day every October. We still go up a few times a year to see how things are getting on. The first proper crop is perhaps three years away, and we've already been promised a bottle of the perry.

draft.title: Replanting a community orchard in Hebden Bridge
draft.excerpt: Forty-two fruit trees, three planting days, a lot of volunteers and quite a lot of cake. A different kind of project for us, and one of our favourites.
draft.body:
Most of our work is for private gardens. Every so often, though, something different comes along, and this was one of those. A residents' group in Hebden Bridge had taken on a steep, neglected field above the town with a handful of old apple trees in it, and they wanted to turn it back into an orchard everyone could use.

They had enthusiasm, a small grant and a great many volunteers. What they didn't have was a plan. That's where we came in.

## Starting with the old trees

There were eleven old trees on the site, mostly apples, a couple of damsons and one very large perry pear that nobody could identify. We had them looked at by a fruit specialist from the Northern Fruit Group, who confirmed that several were old local varieties worth keeping. Two were too far gone and came down. The rest were given a careful restorative prune, spread over three winters so as not to shock them.

## Choosing what to plant

We added forty-two new trees, chosen for three things: they had to be hardy enough for a cold Pennine hillside, they had to be varieties with some link to the north of England, and they had to fruit over a long season so there was always something to pick.

- Apples including 'Ribston Pippin', 'Keswick Codlin', 'Yorkshire Greening' and 'Lord Lambourne'
- Pears 'Hessle' and 'Catillac', both tough and reliable
- Damsons and plums, including 'Shropshire Prune' and 'Victoria'
- A few cobnuts along the top hedge, for the squirrels if nobody else

All of them are on vigorous rootstocks. On an exposed site, they need the strength, and a community orchard benefits from big trees you can stand under.

## The planting days

We ran three planting days in February, each with around thirty volunteers. We gave a short demonstration at the start, then split everyone into small groups, each with someone who had planted a tree before. By the end of the third day every tree was in, staked and guarded against rabbits and deer.

> Someone's grandchild planted the last tree. That felt right.

## The meadow underneath

Between the trees, we've started turning the grass into a wildflower meadow, sown with yellow rattle to weaken the grass, and mown into paths so people can walk through. It'll take a few years to come good. Orchards and meadows both reward patience.

## What happens next

The group now runs pruning workshops each winter and an apple day every October. We still go up a few times a year to see how things are getting on. The first proper crop is perhaps three years away, and we've already been promised a bottle of the perry.

draft.title: A rain garden for a terrace in Headingley
draft.excerpt: A small back yard, a downpipe that flooded the kitchen step every winter, and a planted hollow that now takes all of it.
draft.body:
This one started with a puddle. Not a small one. Every time it rained hard, the downpipe at the back of this Victorian terrace in Headingley sent a sheet of water across the yard and up against the kitchen door. The owners had tried a soakaway, then a bigger soakaway. Neither lasted long in heavy Leeds clay.

What they had was a water problem. What they wanted was a garden. We thought we could give them both.

## How a rain garden works

A rain garden is a shallow planted hollow that catches water from a roof or a hard surface and lets it soak away slowly. It's not a pond. It should be dry most of the time and only hold water for a day or so after heavy rain. The planting has to put up with both: wet feet in winter, dry spells in summer.

The principle is simple. The detail is where it goes right or wrong.

## What we did

1. We disconnected the downpipe from the drain and ran it into a rill, a narrow stone channel across the yard. It turns the rain into something to watch rather than something to dread.
2. At the end of the rill we dug a hollow about 30 centimetres deep, and roughly a fifth of the roof area it drains. On clay, you need more area than you'd think.
3. We dug out the worst of the clay and backfilled with a free-draining mix of topsoil, grit and compost, so water moves down rather than sitting on the surface.
4. An overflow at the low end takes any excess into the old drain, so a summer cloudburst never comes back towards the house.

## Planting for wet and dry

The trick is to plant in zones. The bottom of the hollow, which stays wettest longest, has *Iris sibirica*, *Carex* and *Lythrum*. The sloping sides, which drain faster, have *Geranium* 'Rozanne', *Persicaria* and *Molinia*. The top edge, which barely gets wet at all, has the same plants as the rest of the yard, so the rain garden doesn't look like a separate thing dropped in.

A small multi-stemmed *Amelanchier* gives a bit of height and lovely autumn colour, and it doesn't mind its roots being damp now and then.

## A year on

The kitchen step has stayed dry through two wet winters. The rill runs after every storm, and the owners tell us their daughter goes out in her wellies to watch it. More water stays on site, less goes into an overloaded drain, and a yard that used to be paved and grey now has frogs in it.

> We'd stopped thinking of the back as a garden. Now it's the bit we show people first.

Rain gardens suit small urban spaces very well, and most councils are keen on them. If you've got a downpipe that causes you grief, it might be worth a conversation.

examples.title: Planting tulips and alliums in October
examples.excerpt: Two kinds of bulb, one month and a handful of grit. When to plant, how deep, how far apart, and what to do when they come up in March.
examples.body:
Every April, someone looks at our tulips and tells us they meant to plant some this year. What they meant was October. If you're reading this in October, you've still got time.

## Why October

Bulbs want soil that's cooling down but still workable. In the north, October is when those two overlap: the ground has lost its summer warmth, but it isn't yet cold and sodden, and a trowel still goes in without a fight.

Alliums are the early ones. They're happy to go in from September into October, and the sooner they're in, the sooner they get their roots down.

Tulips are better a little later. Wait until the weather has properly turned, towards the end of the month. Planting into colder soil helps you avoid tulip fire, a fungal disease that spots and twists the leaves and can spoil a whole planting. There's no prize for getting tulips in early. There's quite a big one for getting them in at all.

## How deep, how far apart

Two rules of thumb cover nearly everything. Write them on the back of an envelope and keep it at the potting bench.

- Depth: two to three times the height of the bulb
- Pointy end up (if you really can't tell, lay it on its side and it'll sort itself out)
- Tulips a bit deeper in pots and exposed spots, where the wind rocks tall stems
- Spacing in borders: about two bulb-widths apart
- Spacing in pots: closer, for a fuller look

If you're unsure, go deeper rather than shallower. A deep bulb stands steadier when a cold April wind comes through.

## Pots or borders

Both work. They just ask different things of you.

Pots are mostly about water, and getting rid of it. Make sure there are proper drainage holes, use a gritty compost (or mix a good amount of grit into your usual one), and stand the pots somewhere sheltered from the worst of the winter rain. Lifting them onto pot feet or a couple of bricks stops them sitting in a puddle. A pot that waterlogs in January is a pot of rotten bulbs by March.

Tulips in pots are easiest treated as annuals. Enjoy them, compost them when they're over and start again next autumn. Plenty of tulips dwindle after their first year anyway, so if yours come back, call it a bonus.

In borders, plant in drifts or groups, not single lines. A row of tulips along a path looks like a queue. Dig a wide hole, set a group of bulbs in it, then do the same again a little way off, with uneven gaps between. It looks far more like they meant to be there.

Then mark where they are. A short cane or a label is enough. By July the leaves will have gone and you'll have forgotten, and a spade through a clump of bulbs is a sad way to remember.

Alliums are happy to stay in a border for years. Allium 'Purple Sensation' earns its keep twice: once in flower in late spring, and again when the seedheads stand on through summer.

## A lesson from Corbridge

In the walled garden we've been bringing back near Corbridge, we planted Tulipa 'Ballerina' and Tulipa 'Queen of Night' in the borders in the last week of October, with Allium 'Purple Sensation' between them. Then November was wet. The ground there is heavy clay, and about a third of the tulips rotted. Every single allium came up.

The next autumn we put a handful of grit under each tulip bulb. We lost almost none. If your soil is clay, this is the one step we'd never skip.

## What to do in March

March is when you find out how October went. A few things are worth doing:

- Check pots haven't dried out, or gone the other way and waterlogged
- Watch for shoots coming through, and for slugs, which are very fond of young tulip leaves
- Feed if they look like they need it, especially anything you're hoping to keep for another year
- Note the gaps while you can see them, for next autumn's order

That last one is the job everyone skips. Take a few photos in April when everything's out. In October you won't remember where the bare patch was, and the photos will.

## The short version

- Alliums in now, tulips towards the end of the month
- Two to three times the bulb's height, pointy end up
- Grit in the pots, and under the bulbs on clay
- Drifts, not lines
- A cane where every group went

For the rest of this month's jobs, our piece on what to do in the garden in October has the list. When the weather finally turns, Ten jobs for the first warm weekend picks up where March leaves off.

A spring garden is mostly planted in autumn.

So go and buy some bulbs this month and get them in. And if you'd like a hand with a planting plan for the whole garden, not just the bulbs, it might be worth a conversation.

And if October gets away from you (it usually does), don't leave the tulips in the shed. They'll still go in through November, and often into December, as long as the ground isn't frozen. They may flower a little late. They'll still flower.

draft.title: Meadows are not low-maintenance
draft.excerpt: We love a meadow as much as anyone. But if someone tells you one will look after itself, they're selling you something.
draft.body:
We get asked for meadows a lot. It's easy to see why. A good one in June is about the most beautiful thing a garden can do, full of movement and insects and colour that changes week by week. And there's an idea, which has spread a long way, that you sow some seed, step back and let nature get on with it.

We'd like to gently disagree. Meadows are wonderful. They are not low-maintenance. They're differently maintained, and the work comes at different times of year.

## Start with poor soil

The single biggest reason meadows fail is fertile ground. Wildflowers are adapted to thin, hungry soil. Give them rich garden loam and the grasses romp away and smother everything else within two or three years. On most gardens, that means one of three things:

- Stripping off the top few centimetres of topsoil
- Sowing yellow rattle, a semi-parasitic annual that weakens the grasses
- Or both, which is what we usually recommend

None of these are quick, and the first one involves a lot of wheelbarrows.

## The first year is mostly weeding

A newly sown meadow often looks like a patch of weeds for its first summer. Annual weeds germinate faster than perennial wildflowers, and they need cutting back, sometimes two or three times, so they don't set seed. It's very tempting to give up in July. Don't. Most meadow perennials take a couple of years to flower properly.

## The cut matters more than anything

Once it's established, the main job is the late summer cut. We usually cut in August or early September, once most of the flowers have set seed. Then, and this is the bit people skip, you leave the hay lying for a few days so the seed drops, and then you rake it all off and take it away. Leave it on and it rots down into exactly the fertility you've been trying to avoid.

On a small garden that's an afternoon with a strimmer and a rake. On anything bigger, you'll want someone with the right kit.

> A meadow isn't a lawn you've stopped mowing. It's a crop you harvest once a year.

## Is it worth it?

Yes, nearly always, as long as you go in with your eyes open. A well-managed meadow will be different every year, will feed more insects than almost any other kind of planting, and will need far less from you than a lawn cut every week from April to October.

If a full meadow feels like too much, try a strip of longer grass along a boundary, mown into a path through the middle. It gives you most of the pleasure for a fraction of the work, and you'll learn quickly whether you want more.

examples.title: Planting tulips and alliums in October
examples.excerpt: Two kinds of bulb, one month and a handful of grit. When to plant, how deep, how far apart, and what to do when they come up in March.
examples.body:
Every April, someone looks at our tulips and tells us they meant to plant some this year. What they meant was October. If you're reading this in October, you've still got time.

## Why October

Bulbs want soil that's cooling down but still workable. In the north, October is when those two overlap: the ground has lost its summer warmth, but it isn't yet cold and sodden, and a trowel still goes in without a fight.

Alliums are the early ones. They're happy to go in from September into October, and the sooner they're in, the sooner they get their roots down.

Tulips are better a little later. Wait until the weather has properly turned, towards the end of the month. Planting into colder soil helps you avoid tulip fire, a fungal disease that spots and twists the leaves and can spoil a whole planting. There's no prize for getting tulips in early. There's quite a big one for getting them in at all.

## How deep, how far apart

Two rules of thumb cover nearly everything. Write them on the back of an envelope and keep it at the potting bench.

- Depth: two to three times the height of the bulb
- Pointy end up (if you really can't tell, lay it on its side and it'll sort itself out)
- Tulips a bit deeper in pots and exposed spots, where the wind rocks tall stems
- Spacing in borders: about two bulb-widths apart
- Spacing in pots: closer, for a fuller look

If you're unsure, go deeper rather than shallower. A deep bulb stands steadier when a cold April wind comes through.

## Pots or borders

Both work. They just ask different things of you.

Pots are mostly about water, and getting rid of it. Make sure there are proper drainage holes, use a gritty compost (or mix a good amount of grit into your usual one), and stand the pots somewhere sheltered from the worst of the winter rain. Lifting them onto pot feet or a couple of bricks stops them sitting in a puddle. A pot that waterlogs in January is a pot of rotten bulbs by March.

Tulips in pots are easiest treated as annuals. Enjoy them, compost them when they're over and start again next autumn. Plenty of tulips dwindle after their first year anyway, so if yours come back, call it a bonus.

In borders, plant in drifts or groups, not single lines. A row of tulips along a path looks like a queue. Dig a wide hole, set a group of bulbs in it, then do the same again a little way off, with uneven gaps between. It looks far more like they meant to be there.

Then mark where they are. A short cane or a label is enough. By July the leaves will have gone and you'll have forgotten, and a spade through a clump of bulbs is a sad way to remember.

Alliums are happy to stay in a border for years. Allium 'Purple Sensation' earns its keep twice: once in flower in late spring, and again when the seedheads stand on through summer.

## A lesson from Corbridge

In the walled garden we've been bringing back near Corbridge, we planted Tulipa 'Ballerina' and Tulipa 'Queen of Night' in the borders in the last week of October, with Allium 'Purple Sensation' between them. Then November was wet. The ground there is heavy clay, and about a third of the tulips rotted. Every single allium came up.

The next autumn we put a handful of grit under each tulip bulb. We lost almost none. If your soil is clay, this is the one step we'd never skip.

## What to do in March

March is when you find out how October went. A few things are worth doing:

- Check pots haven't dried out, or gone the other way and waterlogged
- Watch for shoots coming through, and for slugs, which are very fond of young tulip leaves
- Feed if they look like they need it, especially anything you're hoping to keep for another year
- Note the gaps while you can see them, for next autumn's order

That last one is the job everyone skips. Take a few photos in April when everything's out. In October you won't remember where the bare patch was, and the photos will.

## The short version

- Alliums in now, tulips towards the end of the month
- Two to three times the bulb's height, pointy end up
- Grit in the pots, and under the bulbs on clay
- Drifts, not lines
- A cane where every group went

For the rest of this month's jobs, our piece on what to do in the garden in October has the list. When the weather finally turns, Ten jobs for the first warm weekend picks up where March leaves off.

A spring garden is mostly planted in autumn.

So go and buy some bulbs this month and get them in. And if you'd like a hand with a planting plan for the whole garden, not just the bulbs, it might be worth a conversation.

And if October gets away from you (it usually does), don't leave the tulips in the shed. They'll still go in through November, and often into December, as long as the ground isn't frozen. They may flower a little late. They'll still flower.

examples.title: Replanting a community orchard in Hebden Bridge
examples.excerpt: Forty-two fruit trees, three planting days, a lot of volunteers and quite a lot of cake. A different kind of project for us, and one of our favourites.
examples.body:
Most of our work is for private gardens. Every so often, though, something different comes along, and this was one of those. A residents' group in Hebden Bridge had taken on a steep, neglected field above the town with a handful of old apple trees in it, and they wanted to turn it back into an orchard everyone could use.

They had enthusiasm, a small grant and a great many volunteers. What they didn't have was a plan. That's where we came in.

## Starting with the old trees

There were eleven old trees on the site, mostly apples, a couple of damsons and one very large perry pear that nobody could identify. We had them looked at by a fruit specialist from the Northern Fruit Group, who confirmed that several were old local varieties worth keeping. Two were too far gone and came down. The rest were given a careful restorative prune, spread over three winters so as not to shock them.

## Choosing what to plant

We added forty-two new trees, chosen for three things: they had to be hardy enough for a cold Pennine hillside, they had to be varieties with some link to the north of England, and they had to fruit over a long season so there was always something to pick.

- Apples including 'Ribston Pippin', 'Keswick Codlin', 'Yorkshire Greening' and 'Lord Lambourne'
- Pears 'Hessle' and 'Catillac', both tough and reliable
- Damsons and plums, including 'Shropshire Prune' and 'Victoria'
- A few cobnuts along the top hedge, for the squirrels if nobody else

All of them are on vigorous rootstocks. On an exposed site, they need the strength, and a community orchard benefits from big trees you can stand under.

## The planting days

We ran three planting days in February, each with around thirty volunteers. We gave a short demonstration at the start, then split everyone into small groups, each with someone who had planted a tree before. By the end of the third day every tree was in, staked and guarded against rabbits and deer.

> Someone's grandchild planted the last tree. That felt right.

## The meadow underneath

Between the trees, we've started turning the grass into a wildflower meadow, sown with yellow rattle to weaken the grass, and mown into paths so people can walk through. It'll take a few years to come good. Orchards and meadows both reward patience.

## What happens next

The group now runs pruning workshops each winter and an apple day every October. We still go up a few times a year to see how things are getting on. The first proper crop is perhaps three years away, and we've already been promised a bottle of the perry.

draft.title: Meadows are not low-maintenance
draft.excerpt: We love a meadow as much as anyone. But if someone tells you one will look after itself, they're selling you something.
draft.body:
We get asked for meadows a lot. It's easy to see why. A good one in June is about the most beautiful thing a garden can do, full of movement and insects and colour that changes week by week. And there's an idea, which has spread a long way, that you sow some seed, step back and let nature get on with it.

We'd like to gently disagree. Meadows are wonderful. They are not low-maintenance. They're differently maintained, and the work comes at different times of year.

## Start with poor soil

The single biggest reason meadows fail is fertile ground. Wildflowers are adapted to thin, hungry soil. Give them rich garden loam and the grasses romp away and smother everything else within two or three years. On most gardens, that means one of three things:

- Stripping off the top few centimetres of topsoil
- Sowing yellow rattle, a semi-parasitic annual that weakens the grasses
- Or both, which is what we usually recommend

None of these are quick, and the first one involves a lot of wheelbarrows.

## The first year is mostly weeding

A newly sown meadow often looks like a patch of weeds for its first summer. Annual weeds germinate faster than perennial wildflowers, and they need cutting back, sometimes two or three times, so they don't set seed. It's very tempting to give up in July. Don't. Most meadow perennials take a couple of years to flower properly.

draft.title: Planting for salt and wind at Craster
draft.excerpt: A cottage garden a hundred metres from the North Sea, and what we learned about plants that can take a battering.
draft.body:
There's a particular kind of wind you get on the Northumberland coast. It doesn't gust so much as lean. It comes in off the North Sea, carrying salt, and it doesn't stop for days at a time. Anything that grows in a garden at Craster has to put up with it.

Our clients had bought a fisherman's cottage on the edge of the village and wanted a garden that felt as though it belonged there. They'd already lost one round of planting, put in by a previous owner, to the first winter storm. They weren't keen to lose another.

## Shelter first

You can't plant a coastal garden until you've slowed the wind down. A solid wall doesn't help much; the wind goes over the top and comes down hard on the other side. A permeable barrier is far better, because it filters the wind rather than blocking it.

We used a double row of native hedging along the seaward boundary: sea buckthorn, blackthorn and hawthorn, with some *Griselinia* mixed in for evergreen bulk. Until it established, a temporary windbreak of netting on timber posts did the work. It wasn't pretty, but by the second summer the hedge was taller than the netting and we could take it down.

## Plants that cope

Within the shelter, the choice opens up a lot. Plants with grey, silver, waxy or very fine leaves usually handle salt well, because they've evolved to lose less water. The ones that did best for us:

- *Eryngium maritimum*, the sea holly, which looks as though it was designed for exactly this spot
- *Crambe maritima*, sea kale, with big blue leaves and clouds of white flowers
- *Armeria maritima*, thrift, tucked into the dry stone walls
- *Stipa tenuissima* and *Anemanthele*, which bend in the wind rather than snapping
- *Rosa rugosa*, tough as old boots and good for hips in autumn

We avoided anything tall and soft. Delphiniums would have lasted about a week.

## Gravel, not soil

Much of the garden is planted straight into gravel over a free-draining base. It suits the coastal plants, which hate sitting wet, and it keeps weeding down to a manageable level. It also looks right: grey stone, grey-green leaves, the sea beyond.

## Two winters in

The garden has now come through two winters, including a storm that took slates off half the village. Everything survived. The hedge has thickened up, the sea kale has seeded itself into the path, and the owners have started leaving the gate open so walkers on the coast path can look in.

> It looks as if it's always been here. That was the whole point.

If you garden on the coast, the advice is always the same. Shelter first, plant small, and choose things that already grow wild within a mile of you. The sea has been doing the plant trials for a very long time.

examples.title: Planting tulips and alliums in October
examples.excerpt: Two kinds of bulb, one month and a handful of grit. When to plant, how deep, how far apart, and what to do when they come up in March.
examples.body:
Every April, someone looks at our tulips and tells us they meant to plant some this year. What they meant was October. If you're reading this in October, you've still got time.

## Why October

Bulbs want soil that's cooling down but still workable. In the north, October is when those two overlap: the ground has lost its summer warmth, but it isn't yet cold and sodden, and a trowel still goes in without a fight.

Alliums are the early ones. They're happy to go in from September into October, and the sooner they're in, the sooner they get their roots down.

Tulips are better a little later. Wait until the weather has properly turned, towards the end of the month. Planting into colder soil helps you avoid tulip fire, a fungal disease that spots and twists the leaves and can spoil a whole planting. There's no prize for getting tulips in early. There's quite a big one for getting them in at all.

## How deep, how far apart

Two rules of thumb cover nearly everything. Write them on the back of an envelope and keep it at the potting bench.

- Depth: two to three times the height of the bulb
- Pointy end up (if you really can't tell, lay it on its side and it'll sort itself out)
- Tulips a bit deeper in pots and exposed spots, where the wind rocks tall stems
- Spacing in borders: about two bulb-widths apart
- Spacing in pots: closer, for a fuller look

If you're unsure, go deeper rather than shallower. A deep bulb stands steadier when a cold April wind comes through.

## Pots or borders

Both work. They just ask different things of you.

Pots are mostly about water, and getting rid of it. Make sure there are proper drainage holes, use a gritty compost (or mix a good amount of grit into your usual one), and stand the pots somewhere sheltered from the worst of the winter rain. Lifting them onto pot feet or a couple of bricks stops them sitting in a puddle. A pot that waterlogs in January is a pot of rotten bulbs by March.

Tulips in pots are easiest treated as annuals. Enjoy them, compost them when they're over and start again next autumn. Plenty of tulips dwindle after their first year anyway, so if yours come back, call it a bonus.

In borders, plant in drifts or groups, not single lines. A row of tulips along a path looks like a queue. Dig a wide hole, set a group of bulbs in it, then do the same again a little way off, with uneven gaps between. It looks far more like they meant to be there.

Then mark where they are. A short cane or a label is enough. By July the leaves will have gone and you'll have forgotten, and a spade through a clump of bulbs is a sad way to remember.

Alliums are happy to stay in a border for years. Allium 'Purple Sensation' earns its keep twice: once in flower in late spring, and again when the seedheads stand on through summer.

## A lesson from Corbridge

In the walled garden we've been bringing back near Corbridge, we planted Tulipa 'Ballerina' and Tulipa 'Queen of Night' in the borders in the last week of October, with Allium 'Purple Sensation' between them. Then November was wet. The ground there is heavy clay, and about a third of the tulips rotted. Every single allium came up.

The next autumn we put a handful of grit under each tulip bulb. We lost almost none. If your soil is clay, this is the one step we'd never skip.

## What to do in March

March is when you find out how October went. A few things are worth doing:

- Check pots haven't dried out, or gone the other way and waterlogged
- Watch for shoots coming through, and for slugs, which are very fond of young tulip leaves
- Feed if they look like they need it, especially anything you're hoping to keep for another year
- Note the gaps while you can see them, for next autumn's order

That last one is the job everyone skips. Take a few photos in April when everything's out. In October you won't remember where the bare patch was, and the photos will.

## The short version

- Alliums in now, tulips towards the end of the month
- Two to three times the bulb's height, pointy end up
- Grit in the pots, and under the bulbs on clay
- Drifts, not lines
- A cane where every group went

For the rest of this month's jobs, our piece on what to do in the garden in October has the list. When the weather finally turns, Ten jobs for the first warm weekend picks up where March leaves off.

A spring garden is mostly planted in autumn.

So go and buy some bulbs this month and get them in. And if you'd like a hand with a planting plan for the whole garden, not just the bulbs, it might be worth a conversation.

And if October gets away from you (it usually does), don't leave the tulips in the shed. They'll still go in through November, and often into December, as long as the ground isn't frozen. They may flower a little late. They'll still flower.

examples.title: Replanting a community orchard in Hebden Bridge
examples.excerpt: Forty-two fruit trees, three planting days, a lot of volunteers and quite a lot of cake. A different kind of project for us, and one of our favourites.
examples.body:
Most of our work is for private gardens. Every so often, though, something different comes along, and this was one of those. A residents' group in Hebden Bridge had taken on a steep, neglected field above the town with a handful of old apple trees in it, and they wanted to turn it back into an orchard everyone could use.

They had enthusiasm, a small grant and a great many volunteers. What they didn't have was a plan. That's where we came in.

## Starting with the old trees

There were eleven old trees on the site, mostly apples, a couple of damsons and one very large perry pear that nobody could identify. We had them looked at by a fruit specialist from the Northern Fruit Group, who confirmed that several were old local varieties worth keeping. Two were too far gone and came down. The rest were given a careful restorative prune, spread over three winters so as not to shock them.

## Choosing what to plant

We added forty-two new trees, chosen for three things: they had to be hardy enough for a cold Pennine hillside, they had to be varieties with some link to the north of England, and they had to fruit over a long season so there was always something to pick.

- Apples including 'Ribston Pippin', 'Keswick Codlin', 'Yorkshire Greening' and 'Lord Lambourne'
- Pears 'Hessle' and 'Catillac', both tough and reliable
- Damsons and plums, including 'Shropshire Prune' and 'Victoria'
- A few cobnuts along the top hedge, for the squirrels if nobody else

All of them are on vigorous rootstocks. On an exposed site, they need the strength, and a community orchard benefits from big trees you can stand under.

## The planting days

We ran three planting days in February, each with around thirty volunteers. We gave a short demonstration at the start, then split everyone into small groups, each with someone who had planted a tree before. By the end of the third day every tree was in, staked and guarded against rabbits and deer.

> Someone's grandchild planted the last tree. That felt right.

## The meadow underneath

Between the trees, we've started turning the grass into a wildflower meadow, sown with yellow rattle to weaken the grass, and mown into paths so people can walk through. It'll take a few years to come good. Orchards and meadows both reward patience.

## What happens next

The group now runs pruning workshops each winter and an apple day every October. We still go up a few times a year to see how things are getting on. The first proper crop is perhaps three years away, and we've already been promised a bottle of the perry.

You can't plant a coastal garden until you've slowed the wind down. A solid wall doesn't help much; the wind goes over the top and comes down hard on the other side. A permeable barrier is far better, because it filters the wind rather than blocking it.

We used a double row of native hedging along the seaward boundary: sea buckthorn, blackthorn and hawthorn, with some *Griselinia* mixed in for evergreen bulk. Until it established, a temporary windbreak of netting on timber posts did the work. It wasn't pretty, but by the second summer the hedge was taller than the netting and we could take it down.

## Plants that cope

Within the shelter, the choice opens up a lot. Plants with grey, silver, waxy or very fine leaves usually handle salt well, because they've evolved to lose less water. The ones that did best for us:

- *Eryngium maritimum*, the sea holly, which looks as though it was designed for exactly this spot
- *Crambe maritima*, sea kale, with big blue leaves and clouds of white flowers
- *Armeria maritima*, thrift, tucked into the dry stone walls
- *Stipa tenuissima* and *Anemanthele*, which bend in the wind rather than snapping
- *Rosa rugosa*, tough as old boots and good for hips in autumn

We avoided anything tall and soft. Delphiniums would have lasted about a week.

## Gravel, not soil

Much of the garden is planted straight into gravel over a free-draining base. It suits the coastal plants, which hate sitting wet, and it keeps weeding down to a manageable level. It also looks right: grey stone, grey-green leaves, the sea beyond.

## Two winters in

The garden has now come through two winters, including a storm that took slates off half the village. Everything survived. The hedge has thickened up, the sea kale has seeded itself into the path, and the owners have started leaving the gate open so walkers on the coast path can look in.

> It looks as if it's always been here. That was the whole point.

If you garden on the coast, the advice is always the same. Shelter first, plant small, and choose things that already grow wild within a mile of you. The sea has been doing the plant trials for a very long time.

draft.title: What to do in the garden in October
draft.excerpt: The light is going and the borders are going over, but October is one of the most useful months of the year. Here's where we'd spend the time.
draft.body:
October gets a bad press. The clocks are about to go back, the borders look tired, and it's easy to decide the gardening year is over. It isn't. The soil is still warm, there's usually plenty of rain, and anything you plant now has months to get its roots down before it has to do any work. If we could only garden for one month a year, it might well be this one.

## Plant, plant, plant

This is the best time to plant trees, shrubs and hardy perennials. Roots keep growing as long as the soil is above about five degrees, and in most of the country that's well into December. Bare-root hedging and trees start arriving next month and are cheaper than pot-grown, so it's worth getting the ground ready now.

Spring bulbs want to go in too, with one exception. Daffodils, crocus and alliums should be in the ground by the end of the month. Tulips can wait until November, when the colder soil helps keep tulip fire at bay.

## Don't tidy too much

We'll say more about this another time, but the short version is: leave most of it. Seedheads on grasses, *Phlomis*, *Echinacea* and sedums look good with frost on them and feed birds through the winter. Hollow stems give insects somewhere to sleep. Cut back anything that has collapsed into a mush, and leave the rest until February.

## Lift and divide

Perennials that have gone bare in the middle, or that flowered less than they used to, are ready to divide. Dig the whole clump up, split it with two forks back to back (or a sharp spade, if you're feeling decisive), and replant the healthy outer pieces. Throw away the woody centre. Asters, *Geranium*, *Helenium* and most grasses respond well. Leave the grasses that flower late, like *Miscanthus*, until spring.

## A short list for a dry afternoon

1. Clear fallen leaves off the lawn and paths, and stack them in a wire cage to make leaf mould.
2. Give the lawn a last cut with the blades raised.
3. Empty and clean any pots you won't use over winter, so they're ready in spring.
4. Bring tender plants under cover before the first frost, not after it.
5. Clean and sharpen your secateurs. You'll thank yourself in March.

## Keep a note

One last thing. Walk round the garden with a notebook this month and write down what worked and what didn't. The gaps, the plants that sulked, the corner that never gets sun. In April you'll have forgotten, and October is when you can still see it all clearly.

examples.title: Planting tulips and alliums in October
examples.excerpt: Two kinds of bulb, one month and a handful of grit. When to plant, how deep, how far apart, and what to do when they come up in March.
examples.body:
Every April, someone looks at our tulips and tells us they meant to plant some this year. What they meant was October. If you're reading this in October, you've still got time.

## Why October

Bulbs want soil that's cooling down but still workable. In the north, October is when those two overlap: the ground has lost its summer warmth, but it isn't yet cold and sodden, and a trowel still goes in without a fight.

Alliums are the early ones. They're happy to go in from September into October, and the sooner they're in, the sooner they get their roots down.

Tulips are better a little later. Wait until the weather has properly turned, towards the end of the month. Planting into colder soil helps you avoid tulip fire, a fungal disease that spots and twists the leaves and can spoil a whole planting. There's no prize for getting tulips in early. There's quite a big one for getting them in at all.

## How deep, how far apart

Two rules of thumb cover nearly everything. Write them on the back of an envelope and keep it at the potting bench.

- Depth: two to three times the height of the bulb
- Pointy end up (if you really can't tell, lay it on its side and it'll sort itself out)
- Tulips a bit deeper in pots and exposed spots, where the wind rocks tall stems
- Spacing in borders: about two bulb-widths apart
- Spacing in pots: closer, for a fuller look

If you're unsure, go deeper rather than shallower. A deep bulb stands steadier when a cold April wind comes through.

## Pots or borders

Both work. They just ask different things of you.

Pots are mostly about water, and getting rid of it. Make sure there are proper drainage holes, use a gritty compost (or mix a good amount of grit into your usual one), and stand the pots somewhere sheltered from the worst of the winter rain. Lifting them onto pot feet or a couple of bricks stops them sitting in a puddle. A pot that waterlogs in January is a pot of rotten bulbs by March.

Tulips in pots are easiest treated as annuals. Enjoy them, compost them when they're over and start again next autumn. Plenty of tulips dwindle after their first year anyway, so if yours come back, call it a bonus.

In borders, plant in drifts or groups, not single lines. A row of tulips along a path looks like a queue. Dig a wide hole, set a group of bulbs in it, then do the same again a little way off, with uneven gaps between. It looks far more like they meant to be there.

Then mark where they are. A short cane or a label is enough. By July the leaves will have gone and you'll have forgotten, and a spade through a clump of bulbs is a sad way to remember.

Alliums are happy to stay in a border for years. Allium 'Purple Sensation' earns its keep twice: once in flower in late spring, and again when the seedheads stand on through summer.

## A lesson from Corbridge

In the walled garden we've been bringing back near Corbridge, we planted Tulipa 'Ballerina' and Tulipa 'Queen of Night' in the borders in the last week of October, with Allium 'Purple Sensation' between them. Then November was wet. The ground there is heavy clay, and about a third of the tulips rotted. Every single allium came up.

The next autumn we put a handful of grit under each tulip bulb. We lost almost none. If your soil is clay, this is the one step we'd never skip.

## What to do in March

March is when you find out how October went. A few things are worth doing:

- Check pots haven't dried out, or gone the other way and waterlogged
- Watch for shoots coming through, and for slugs, which are very fond of young tulip leaves
- Feed if they look like they need it, especially anything you're hoping to keep for another year
- Note the gaps while you can see them, for next autumn's order

That last one is the job everyone skips. Take a few photos in April when everything's out. In October you won't remember where the bare patch was, and the photos will.

## The short version

- Alliums in now, tulips towards the end of the month
- Two to three times the bulb's height, pointy end up
- Grit in the pots, and under the bulbs on clay
- Drifts, not lines
- A cane where every group went

For the rest of this month's jobs, our piece on what to do in the garden in October has the list. When the weather finally turns, Ten jobs for the first warm weekend picks up where March leaves off.

A spring garden is mostly planted in autumn.

So go and buy some bulbs this month and get them in. And if you'd like a hand with a planting plan for the whole garden, not just the bulbs, it might be worth a conversation.

And if October gets away from you (it usually does), don't leave the tulips in the shed. They'll still go in through November, and often into December, as long as the ground isn't frozen. They may flower a little late. They'll still flower.

examples.title: Replanting a community orchard in Hebden Bridge
examples.excerpt: Forty-two fruit trees, three planting days, a lot of volunteers and quite a lot of cake. A different kind of project for us, and one of our favourites.
examples.body:
Most of our work is for private gardens. Every so often, though, something different comes along, and this was one of those. A residents' group in Hebden Bridge had taken on a steep, neglected field above the town with a handful of old apple trees in it, and they wanted to turn it back into an orchard everyone could use.

They had enthusiasm, a small grant and a great many volunteers. What they didn't have was a plan. That's where we came in.

## Starting with the old trees

There were eleven old trees on the site, mostly apples, a couple of damsons and one very large perry pear that nobody could identify. We had them looked at by a fruit specialist from the Northern Fruit Group, who confirmed that several were old local varieties worth keeping. Two were too far gone and came down. The rest were given a careful restorative prune, spread over three winters so as not to shock them.

## Choosing what to plant

We added forty-two new trees, chosen for three things: they had to be hardy enough for a cold Pennine hillside, they had to be varieties with some link to the north of England, and they had to fruit over a long season so there was always something to pick.

- Apples including 'Ribston Pippin', 'Keswick Codlin', 'Yorkshire Greening' and 'Lord Lambourne'
- Pears 'Hessle' and 'Catillac', both tough and reliable
- Damsons and plums, including 'Shropshire Prune' and 'Victoria'
- A few cobnuts along the top hedge, for the squirrels if nobody else

All of them are on vigorous rootstocks. On an exposed site, they need the strength, and a community orchard benefits from big trees you can stand under.

## The planting days

We ran three planting days in February, each with around thirty volunteers. We gave a short demonstration at the start, then split everyone into small groups, each with someone who had planted a tree before. By the end of the third day every tree was in, staked and guarded against rabbits and deer.

> Someone's grandchild planted the last tree. That felt right.

## The meadow underneath

Between the trees, we've started turning the grass into a wildflower meadow, sown with yellow rattle to weaken the grass, and mown into paths so people can walk through. It'll take a few years to come good. Orchards and meadows both reward patience.

## What happens next

The group now runs pruning workshops each winter and an apple day every October. We still go up a few times a year to see how things are getting on. The first proper crop is perhaps three years away, and we've already been promised a bottle of the perry.

The soil is still warm, there's usually plenty of rain, and anything you plant now has months to get its roots down before it has to do any work. If we could only garden for one month a year, it might well be this one.
Plant, plant, plant

This is the best time to plant trees, shrubs and hardy perennials. Roots keep growing as long as the soil is above about five degrees, and in most of the country that's well into December. Bare-root hedging and trees start arriving next month and are cheaper than pot-grown, so it's worth getting the ground ready now.

Spring bulbs want to go in too, with one exception. Daffodils, crocus and alliums should be in the ground by the end of the month. Tulips can wait until November, when the colder soil helps keep tulip fire at bay.
Don't tidy too much
We'll say more about this another time, but the short version is: leave most of it. Seedheads on grasses,
Phlomis
Echinacea

and sedums look good with frost on them and feed birds through the winter. Hollow stems give insects somewhere to sleep. Cut back anything that has collapsed into a mush, and leave the rest until February.
Lift and divide

Perennials that have gone bare in the middle, or that flowered less than they used to, are ready to divide. Dig the whole clump up, split it with two forks back to back (or a sharp spade, if you're feeling decisive), and replant the healthy outer pieces. Throw away the woody centre. Asters,
Geranium
Helenium
and most grasses respond well. Leave the grasses that flower late, like
Miscanthus
, until spring.
A short list for a dry afternoon
Clear fallen leaves off the lawn and paths, and stack them in a wire cage to make leaf mould.
Give the lawn a last cut with the blades raised.
Empty and clean any pots you won't use over winter, so they're ready in spring.
Bring tender plants under cover before the first frost, not after it.
Clean and sharpen your secateurs. You'll thank yourself in March.
Keep a note

One last thing. Walk round the garden with a notebook this month and write down what worked and what didn't. The gaps, the plants that sulked, the corner that never gets sun. In April you'll have forgotten, and October is when you can still see it all clearly.

draft.title: Bringing back a walled garden near Corbridge
draft.excerpt: Two years, one very old wall and a lot of bindweed. How we turned a forgotten kitchen garden into somewhere a family actually uses.
draft.body:
When we first pushed open the door into this garden, it stuck halfway on a root. That set the tone. The walls were sound, mostly, but everything inside them had been left to its own devices for the best part of thirty years. Sycamore seedlings had become trees. The glasshouse had lost most of its glass. And the bindweed had got everywhere, as bindweed does.

The owners didn't want a museum piece. They have two children and a dog, and they wanted a garden they would walk into every day, not one they'd feel guilty about. So we started with a simple question: what do you actually want to do in here?

## What they asked for

The list was short, which we liked.

- Somewhere to grow vegetables without it taking over every weekend
- A long table for summer lunches, out of the wind
- Something to look at from the kitchen window in January
- Room for the children to run about without flattening anything precious

## Working with the walls

Old walls hold heat. A south-facing brick wall in Northumberland can be a couple of degrees warmer than open ground, which is the difference between a pear that ripens and one that doesn't. We repointed the worst sections with lime mortar, kept the old vine eyes where we could, and trained espalier pears and a fig along the warmest stretch.

The cross paths were still there under the turf, which told us where the original beds had been. We followed them. It's tempting to impose a new layout on a place like this, but the old one usually exists for a reason, and here it gave us four good-sized quarters and a central dipping pond that only needed relining.

## Planting

Two quarters went to vegetables, in raised beds edged with oak boards. Raised beds aren't always the answer, but here the soil was so full of bindweed root that starting clean was the only sensible option. The other two quarters are a mix of cutting flowers and perennials: a lot of *Sanguisorba*, *Persicaria* and late asters, with tulips for spring that the family can cut without feeling they're ruining anything.

> "We eat out here most evenings now. I didn't think that would ever happen in this part of the world." — the owners, a year on

The long table sits against the north wall, facing the sun, with a pleached hornbeam screen behind it. It's the warmest seat in the garden from April to October.

## What we'd do differently

We'd have rebuilt the glasshouse sooner. We left it until the second year to spread the cost, and it meant a season of raising seedlings on the kitchen windowsill. Worth knowing if you're planning something similar: the glasshouse is the engine of a kitchen garden, and everything else runs better once it's working.

If you have an old walled garden and aren't sure where to start, we're always happy to come and have a look. Bring wellies.

examples.title: Planting tulips and alliums in October
examples.excerpt: Two kinds of bulb, one month and a handful of grit. When to plant, how deep, how far apart, and what to do when they come up in March.
examples.body:
Every April, someone looks at our tulips and tells us they meant to plant some this year. What they meant was October. If you're reading this in October, you've still got time.

## Why October

Bulbs want soil that's cooling down but still workable. In the north, October is when those two overlap: the ground has lost its summer warmth, but it isn't yet cold and sodden, and a trowel still goes in without a fight.

Alliums are the early ones. They're happy to go in from September into October, and the sooner they're in, the sooner they get their roots down.

Tulips are better a little later. Wait until the weather has properly turned, towards the end of the month. Planting into colder soil helps you avoid tulip fire, a fungal disease that spots and twists the leaves and can spoil a whole planting. There's no prize for getting tulips in early. There's quite a big one for getting them in at all.

## How deep, how far apart

Two rules of thumb cover nearly everything. Write them on the back of an envelope and keep it at the potting bench.

- Depth: two to three times the height of the bulb
- Pointy end up (if you really can't tell, lay it on its side and it'll sort itself out)
- Tulips a bit deeper in pots and exposed spots, where the wind rocks tall stems
- Spacing in borders: about two bulb-widths apart
- Spacing in pots: closer, for a fuller look

If you're unsure, go deeper rather than shallower. A deep bulb stands steadier when a cold April wind comes through.

## Pots or borders

Both work. They just ask different things of you.

Pots are mostly about water, and getting rid of it. Make sure there are proper drainage holes, use a gritty compost (or mix a good amount of grit into your usual one), and stand the pots somewhere sheltered from the worst of the winter rain. Lifting them onto pot feet or a couple of bricks stops them sitting in a puddle. A pot that waterlogs in January is a pot of rotten bulbs by March.

Tulips in pots are easiest treated as annuals. Enjoy them, compost them when they're over and start again next autumn. Plenty of tulips dwindle after their first year anyway, so if yours come back, call it a bonus.

In borders, plant in drifts or groups, not single lines. A row of tulips along a path looks like a queue. Dig a wide hole, set a group of bulbs in it, then do the same again a little way off, with uneven gaps between. It looks far more like they meant to be there.

Then mark where they are. A short cane or a label is enough. By July the leaves will have gone and you'll have forgotten, and a spade through a clump of bulbs is a sad way to remember.

Alliums are happy to stay in a border for years. Allium 'Purple Sensation' earns its keep twice: once in flower in late spring, and again when the seedheads stand on through summer.

## A lesson from Corbridge

In the walled garden we've been bringing back near Corbridge, we planted Tulipa 'Ballerina' and Tulipa 'Queen of Night' in the borders in the last week of October, with Allium 'Purple Sensation' between them. Then November was wet. The ground there is heavy clay, and about a third of the tulips rotted. Every single allium came up.

The next autumn we put a handful of grit under each tulip bulb. We lost almost none. If your soil is clay, this is the one step we'd never skip.

## What to do in March

March is when you find out how October went. A few things are worth doing:

- Check pots haven't dried out, or gone the other way and waterlogged
- Watch for shoots coming through, and for slugs, which are very fond of young tulip leaves
- Feed if they look like they need it, especially anything you're hoping to keep for another year
- Note the gaps while you can see them, for next autumn's order

That last one is the job everyone skips. Take a few photos in April when everything's out. In October you won't remember where the bare patch was, and the photos will.

## The short version

- Alliums in now, tulips towards the end of the month
- Two to three times the bulb's height, pointy end up
- Grit in the pots, and under the bulbs on clay
- Drifts, not lines
- A cane where every group went

For the rest of this month's jobs, our piece on what to do in the garden in October has the list. When the weather finally turns, Ten jobs for the first warm weekend picks up where March leaves off.

A spring garden is mostly planted in autumn.

So go and buy some bulbs this month and get them in. And if you'd like a hand with a planting plan for the whole garden, not just the bulbs, it might be worth a conversation.

And if October gets away from you (it usually does), don't leave the tulips in the shed. They'll still go in through November, and often into December, as long as the ground isn't frozen. They may flower a little late. They'll still flower.

examples.title: Replanting a community orchard in Hebden Bridge
examples.excerpt: Forty-two fruit trees, three planting days, a lot of volunteers and quite a lot of cake. A different kind of project for us, and one of our favourites.
examples.body:
Most of our work is for private gardens. Every so often, though, something different comes along, and this was one of those. A residents' group in Hebden Bridge had taken on a steep, neglected field above the town with a handful of old apple trees in it, and they wanted to turn it back into an orchard everyone could use.

They had enthusiasm, a small grant and a great many volunteers. What they didn't have was a plan. That's where we came in.

## Starting with the old trees

There were eleven old trees on the site, mostly apples, a couple of damsons and one very large perry pear that nobody could identify. We had them looked at by a fruit specialist from the Northern Fruit Group, who confirmed that several were old local varieties worth keeping. Two were too far gone and came down. The rest were given a careful restorative prune, spread over three winters so as not to shock them.

## Choosing what to plant

We added forty-two new trees, chosen for three things: they had to be hardy enough for a cold Pennine hillside, they had to be varieties with some link to the north of England, and they had to fruit over a long season so there was always something to pick.

- Apples including 'Ribston Pippin', 'Keswick Codlin', 'Yorkshire Greening' and 'Lord Lambourne'
- Pears 'Hessle' and 'Catillac', both tough and reliable
- Damsons and plums, including 'Shropshire Prune' and 'Victoria'
- A few cobnuts along the top hedge, for the squirrels if nobody else

All of them are on vigorous rootstocks. On an exposed site, they need the strength, and a community orchard benefits from big trees you can stand under.

## The planting days

We ran three planting days in February, each with around thirty volunteers. We gave a short demonstration at the start, then split everyone into small groups, each with someone who had planted a tree before. By the end of the third day every tree was in, staked and guarded against rabbits and deer.

> Someone's grandchild planted the last tree. That felt right.

## The meadow underneath

Between the trees, we've started turning the grass into a wildflower meadow, sown with yellow rattle to weaken the grass, and mown into paths so people can walk through. It'll take a few years to come good. Orchards and meadows both reward patience.

## What happens next

The group now runs pruning workshops each winter and an apple day every October. We still go up a few times a year to see how things are getting on. The first proper crop is perhaps three years away, and we've already been promised a bottle of the perry.

Sanguisorba
Persicaria
and late asters, with tulips for spring that the family can cut without feeling they're ruining anything.

draft.excerpt: Almost every garden has room for a tree. These are the five we come back to most often when space is tight.
draft.body:
"We haven't got room for a tree." We hear it a lot, and it's almost never true. A well-chosen tree gives a small garden height, shade, a bit of privacy and something to look at in every season. The trick is choosing one that stays in proportion and earns its keep all year.

Bare-root season is starting, so this is a good time to think about it. These are the five we plant most often in small gardens.

## 1. Amelanchier lamarckii

Our default, if we're honest. White blossom in April, bronze new leaves, small dark berries the birds love in June, and properly fiery autumn colour. It grows to around six metres, slowly, and is often sold multi-stemmed, which suits a small space better than a single trunk. It's fine in most soils and takes partial shade.

## 2. Malus 'Evereste'

A crab apple with pink buds opening to white blossom, then small orange-red fruit that hang on well into winter. It's a good pollinator for any eating apples nearby, and it fits comfortably into a garden twenty metres long. If you want one tree that does something in every season, this is a strong candidate.

## 3. Cornus kousa

Slower and a little more fussy, preferring neutral to acid soil, but worth it. The flowers in June are really bracts, creamy white and held flat along the branches, so the whole tree looks layered. Strawberry-like fruit and good autumn colour follow. Give it a sheltered spot.

## 4. Sorbus 'Joseph Rock'

A rowan with an upright habit, which makes it useful where you don't have much width. Clusters of pale yellow berries in autumn and leaves that turn red and purple. It copes well in colder, exposed gardens, which matters to us up here.

## 5. Acer griseum

The paper-bark maple. It's grown mainly for its bark, which peels in thin cinnamon-coloured curls and glows when the sun is low. It's slow and stays small for years. Plant it where you'll see it from the house in winter, ideally with light behind it.

## A few things to bear in mind

- Look at the size after ten years, not the eventual height. Most of these will take decades to reach the maximum.
- Think about where the shade will fall in summer, and whether you want it there.
- Plant at the same depth it was growing, not deeper. The flare at the base of the trunk should sit just above the soil.
- Water it through its first two summers. This is the step people forget.

If you'd like help choosing, we're always happy to talk trees. It's one of our favourite conversations.

examples.title: Planting tulips and alliums in October
examples.excerpt: Two kinds of bulb, one month and a handful of grit. When to plant, how deep, how far apart, and what to do when they come up in March.
examples.body:
Every April, someone looks at our tulips and tells us they meant to plant some this year. What they meant was October. If you're reading this in October, you've still got time.

## Why October

Bulbs want soil that's cooling down but still workable. In the north, October is when those two overlap: the ground has lost its summer warmth, but it isn't yet cold and sodden, and a trowel still goes in without a fight.

Alliums are the early ones. They're happy to go in from September into October, and the sooner they're in, the sooner they get their roots down.

Tulips are better a little later. Wait until the weather has properly turned, towards the end of the month. Planting into colder soil helps you avoid tulip fire, a fungal disease that spots and twists the leaves and can spoil a whole planting. There's no prize for getting tulips in early. There's quite a big one for getting them in at all.

## How deep, how far apart

Two rules of thumb cover nearly everything. Write them on the back of an envelope and keep it at the potting bench.

- Depth: two to three times the height of the bulb
- Pointy end up (if you really can't tell, lay it on its side and it'll sort itself out)
- Tulips a bit deeper in pots and exposed spots, where the wind rocks tall stems
- Spacing in borders: about two bulb-widths apart
- Spacing in pots: closer, for a fuller look

If you're unsure, go deeper rather than shallower. A deep bulb stands steadier when a cold April wind comes through.

## Pots or borders

Both work. They just ask different things of you.

Pots are mostly about water, and getting rid of it. Make sure there are proper drainage holes, use a gritty compost (or mix a good amount of grit into your usual one), and stand the pots somewhere sheltered from the worst of the winter rain. Lifting them onto pot feet or a couple of bricks stops them sitting in a puddle. A pot that waterlogs in January is a pot of rotten bulbs by March.

Tulips in pots are easiest treated as annuals. Enjoy them, compost them when they're over and start again next autumn. Plenty of tulips dwindle after their first year anyway, so if yours come back, call it a bonus.

In borders, plant in drifts or groups, not single lines. A row of tulips along a path looks like a queue. Dig a wide hole, set a group of bulbs in it, then do the same again a little way off, with uneven gaps between. It looks far more like they meant to be there.

Then mark where they are. A short cane or a label is enough. By July the leaves will have gone and you'll have forgotten, and a spade through a clump of bulbs is a sad way to remember.

Alliums are happy to stay in a border for years. Allium 'Purple Sensation' earns its keep twice: once in flower in late spring, and again when the seedheads stand on through summer.

## A lesson from Corbridge

In the walled garden we've been bringing back near Corbridge, we planted Tulipa 'Ballerina' and Tulipa 'Queen of Night' in the borders in the last week of October, with Allium 'Purple Sensation' between them. Then November was wet. The ground there is heavy clay, and about a third of the tulips rotted. Every single allium came up.

The next autumn we put a handful of grit under each tulip bulb. We lost almost none. If your soil is clay, this is the one step we'd never skip.

## What to do in March

March is when you find out how October went. A few things are worth doing:

- Check pots haven't dried out, or gone the other way and waterlogged
- Watch for shoots coming through, and for slugs, which are very fond of young tulip leaves
- Feed if they look like they need it, especially anything you're hoping to keep for another year
- Note the gaps while you can see them, for next autumn's order

That last one is the job everyone skips. Take a few photos in April when everything's out. In October you won't remember where the bare patch was, and the photos will.

## The short version

- Alliums in now, tulips towards the end of the month
- Two to three times the bulb's height, pointy end up
- Grit in the pots, and under the bulbs on clay
- Drifts, not lines
- A cane where every group went

For the rest of this month's jobs, our piece on what to do in the garden in October has the list. When the weather finally turns, Ten jobs for the first warm weekend picks up where March leaves off.

A spring garden is mostly planted in autumn.

So go and buy some bulbs this month and get them in. And if you'd like a hand with a planting plan for the whole garden, not just the bulbs, it might be worth a conversation.

And if October gets away from you (it usually does), don't leave the tulips in the shed. They'll still go in through November, and often into December, as long as the ground isn't frozen. They may flower a little late. They'll still flower.

examples.title: Replanting a community orchard in Hebden Bridge
examples.excerpt: Forty-two fruit trees, three planting days, a lot of volunteers and quite a lot of cake. A different kind of project for us, and one of our favourites.
examples.body:
Most of our work is for private gardens. Every so often, though, something different comes along, and this was one of those. A residents' group in Hebden Bridge had taken on a steep, neglected field above the town with a handful of old apple trees in it, and they wanted to turn it back into an orchard everyone could use.

They had enthusiasm, a small grant and a great many volunteers. What they didn't have was a plan. That's where we came in.

## Starting with the old trees

There were eleven old trees on the site, mostly apples, a couple of damsons and one very large perry pear that nobody could identify. We had them looked at by a fruit specialist from the Northern Fruit Group, who confirmed that several were old local varieties worth keeping. Two were too far gone and came down. The rest were given a careful restorative prune, spread over three winters so as not to shock them.

## Choosing what to plant

We added forty-two new trees, chosen for three things: they had to be hardy enough for a cold Pennine hillside, they had to be varieties with some link to the north of England, and they had to fruit over a long season so there was always something to pick.

- Apples including 'Ribston Pippin', 'Keswick Codlin', 'Yorkshire Greening' and 'Lord Lambourne'
- Pears 'Hessle' and 'Catillac', both tough and reliable
- Damsons and plums, including 'Shropshire Prune' and 'Victoria'
- A few cobnuts along the top hedge, for the squirrels if nobody else

All of them are on vigorous rootstocks. On an exposed site, they need the strength, and a community orchard benefits from big trees you can stand under.

## The planting days

We ran three planting days in February, each with around thirty volunteers. We gave a short demonstration at the start, then split everyone into small groups, each with someone who had planted a tree before. By the end of the third day every tree was in, staked and guarded against rabbits and deer.

> Someone's grandchild planted the last tree. That felt right.

## The meadow underneath

Between the trees, we've started turning the grass into a wildflower meadow, sown with yellow rattle to weaken the grass, and mown into paths so people can walk through. It'll take a few years to come good. Orchards and meadows both reward patience.

## What happens next

The group now runs pruning workshops each winter and an apple day every October. We still go up a few times a year to see how things are getting on. The first proper crop is perhaps three years away, and we've already been promised a bottle of the perry.

draft.title: Why we leave the seedheads standing
draft.excerpt: A tidy border in December is an empty one. Why we ask clients to hold off with the shears until late winter, and what they get in return.
draft.body:
Every year, around the end of November, we get the same email from at least one client. It usually starts politely and ends with a question about whether we've forgotten to cut the borders back. We haven't. We've left them standing on purpose, and we'd like to explain why.

## They look good

This is the reason people find easiest to believe once they've seen it. A border of grasses and strong-stemmed perennials, left alone, holds its shape right through winter. On a frosty morning, with low sun coming through the *Calamagrostis* and every seedhead outlined in white, it can look better than it did in July. Cut it all to the ground in November and you have four months of bare soil instead.

Not everything earns its place. Some plants collapse into a slimy heap at the first hard frost, and those can go. But a surprising number stand up well:

- *Calamagrostis* 'Karl Foerster', which stays upright almost until spring
- *Phlomis russeliana*, with its tiers of round seedheads
- *Echinacea* and *Rudbeckia*, which go dark and architectural
- *Eryngium*, *Veronicastrum* and most of the sedums

## They feed things

Goldfinches will strip a teasel or a stand of *Echinacea* in an afternoon. Blue tits work through seedheads looking for insects. On one garden in Hexham, the owners counted more birds in the border in January than in any summer month, which surprised them and, if we're honest, surprised us a little too.

## They shelter things
