examples.title: Planting tulips and alliums in October
examples.excerpt: Two kinds of bulb, one month and a handful of grit. When to plant, how deep, how far apart, and what to do when they come up in March.
examples.body:
Every April, someone looks at our tulips and tells us they meant to plant some this year. What they meant was October. If you're reading this in October, you've still got time.

## Why October

Bulbs want soil that's cooling down but still workable. In the north, October is when those two overlap: the ground has lost its summer warmth, but it isn't yet cold and sodden, and a trowel still goes in without a fight.

Alliums are the early ones. They're happy to go in from September into October, and the sooner they're in, the sooner they get their roots down.

Tulips are better a little later. Wait until the weather has properly turned, towards the end of the month. Planting into colder soil helps you avoid tulip fire, a fungal disease that spots and twists the leaves and can spoil a whole planting. There's no prize for getting tulips in early. There's quite a big one for getting them in at all.

## How deep, how far apart

Two rules of thumb cover nearly everything. Write them on the back of an envelope and keep it at the potting bench.

- Depth: two to three times the height of the bulb
- Pointy end up (if you really can't tell, lay it on its side and it'll sort itself out)
- Tulips a bit deeper in pots and exposed spots, where the wind rocks tall stems
- Spacing in borders: about two bulb-widths apart
- Spacing in pots: closer, for a fuller look

If you're unsure, go deeper rather than shallower. A deep bulb stands steadier when a cold April wind comes through.

## Pots or borders

Both work. They just ask different things of you.

Pots are mostly about water, and getting rid of it. Make sure there are proper drainage holes, use a gritty compost (or mix a good amount of grit into your usual one), and stand the pots somewhere sheltered from the worst of the winter rain. Lifting them onto pot feet or a couple of bricks stops them sitting in a puddle. A pot that waterlogs in January is a pot of rotten bulbs by March.

Tulips in pots are easiest treated as annuals. Enjoy them, compost them when they're over and start again next autumn. Plenty of tulips dwindle after their first year anyway, so if yours come back, call it a bonus.

In borders, plant in drifts or groups, not single lines. A row of tulips along a path looks like a queue. Dig a wide hole, set a group of bulbs in it, then do the same again a little way off, with uneven gaps between. It looks far more like they meant to be there.

Then mark where they are. A short cane or a label is enough. By July the leaves will have gone and you'll have forgotten, and a spade through a clump of bulbs is a sad way to remember.

Alliums are happy to stay in a border for years. Allium 'Purple Sensation' earns its keep twice: once in flower in late spring, and again when the seedheads stand on through summer.

## A lesson from Corbridge

In the walled garden we've been bringing back near Corbridge, we planted Tulipa 'Ballerina' and Tulipa 'Queen of Night' in the borders in the last week of October, with Allium 'Purple Sensation' between them. Then November was wet. The ground there is heavy clay, and about a third of the tulips rotted. Every single allium came up.

The next autumn we put a handful of grit under each tulip bulb. We lost almost none. If your soil is clay, this is the one step we'd never skip.

## What to do in March

March is when you find out how October went. A few things are worth doing:

- Check pots haven't dried out, or gone the other way and waterlogged
- Watch for shoots coming through, and for slugs, which are very fond of young tulip leaves
- Feed if they look like they need it, especially anything you're hoping to keep for another year
- Note the gaps while you can see them, for next autumn's order

That last one is the job everyone skips. Take a few photos in April when everything's out. In October you won't remember where the bare patch was, and the photos will.

## The short version

- Alliums in now, tulips towards the end of the month
- Two to three times the bulb's height, pointy end up
- Grit in the pots, and under the bulbs on clay
- Drifts, not lines
- A cane where every group went

For the rest of this month's jobs, our piece on what to do in the garden in October has the list. When the weather finally turns, Ten jobs for the first warm weekend picks up where March leaves off.

A spring garden is mostly planted in autumn.

So go and buy some bulbs this month and get them in. And if you'd like a hand with a planting plan for the whole garden, not just the bulbs, it might be worth a conversation.

And if October gets away from you (it usually does), don't leave the tulips in the shed. They'll still go in through November, and often into December, as long as the ground isn't frozen. They may flower a little late. They'll still flower.

examples.title: Replanting a community orchard in Hebden Bridge
examples.excerpt: Forty-two fruit trees, three planting days, a lot of volunteers and quite a lot of cake. A different kind of project for us, and one of our favourites.
examples.body:
Most of our work is for private gardens. Every so often, though, something different comes along, and this was one of those. A residents' group in Hebden Bridge had taken on a steep, neglected field above the town with a handful of old apple trees in it, and they wanted to turn it back into an orchard everyone could use.

They had enthusiasm, a small grant and a great many volunteers. What they didn't have was a plan. That's where we came in.

## Starting with the old trees

There were eleven old trees on the site, mostly apples, a couple of damsons and one very large perry pear that nobody could identify. We had them looked at by a fruit specialist from the Northern Fruit Group, who confirmed that several were old local varieties worth keeping. Two were too far gone and came down. The rest were given a careful restorative prune, spread over three winters so as not to shock them.

## Choosing what to plant

We added forty-two new trees, chosen for three things: they had to be hardy enough for a cold Pennine hillside, they had to be varieties with some link to the north of England, and they had to fruit over a long season so there was always something to pick.

- Apples including 'Ribston Pippin', 'Keswick Codlin', 'Yorkshire Greening' and 'Lord Lambourne'
- Pears 'Hessle' and 'Catillac', both tough and reliable
- Damsons and plums, including 'Shropshire Prune' and 'Victoria'
- A few cobnuts along the top hedge, for the squirrels if nobody else

All of them are on vigorous rootstocks. On an exposed site, they need the strength, and a community orchard benefits from big trees you can stand under.

## The planting days

We ran three planting days in February, each with around thirty volunteers. We gave a short demonstration at the start, then split everyone into small groups, each with someone who had planted a tree before. By the end of the third day every tree was in, staked and guarded against rabbits and deer.

> Someone's grandchild planted the last tree. That felt right.

## The meadow underneath

Between the trees, we've started turning the grass into a wildflower meadow, sown with yellow rattle to weaken the grass, and mown into paths so people can walk through. It'll take a few years to come good. Orchards and meadows both reward patience.

## What happens next

The group now runs pruning workshops each winter and an apple day every October. We still go up a few times a year to see how things are getting on. The first proper crop is perhaps three years away, and we've already been promised a bottle of the perry.

data.title: Why we leave the seedheads standing
data.excerpt: A tidy border in December is an empty one. Why we ask clients to hold off with the shears until late winter, and what they get in return.

content.text: Every year, around the end of November, we get the same email from at least one client. It usually starts politely and ends with a question about whether we've forgotten to cut the borders back. We haven't. We've left them standing on purpose, and we'd like to explain why.
They look good

This is the reason people find easiest to believe once they've seen it. A border of grasses and strong-stemmed perennials, left alone, holds its shape right through winter. On a frosty morning, with low sun coming through the
Calamagrostis
and every seedhead outlined in white, it can look better than it did in July. Cut it all to the ground in November and you have four months of bare soil instead.
Not everything earns its place. Some plants collapse into a slimy heap at the first hard frost, and those can go. But a surprising number stand up well:
Calamagrostis
'Karl Foerster', which stays upright almost until spring
Phlomis russeliana
, with its tiers of round seedheads
Echinacea
and
Rudbeckia
, which go dark and architectural
Eryngium
Veronicastrum
and most of the sedums
They feed things
Goldfinches will strip a teasel or a stand of
Echinacea

in an afternoon. Blue tits work through seedheads looking for insects. On one garden in Hexham, the owners counted more birds in the border in January than in any summer month, which surprised them and, if we're honest, surprised us a little too.
They shelter things

Hollow stems are where solitary bees and other insects spend the winter. Leaf litter at the base of plants protects ladybirds and beetles that will be eating your aphids in May. Clear the lot and you clear them out too, then wonder why the greenfly arrive before anything else does.

So when do we cut back?

Late February or early March, depending on the year. We wait until the worst of the frosts have passed but before new growth is far enough along to get damaged. A sharp pair of shears, or a hedge trimmer on the bigger grasses, makes short work of it. Most of what comes off can be chopped and laid back on the border as a mulch, or put on the compost heap.

If the idea of a whole winter of standing stems is too much, there's a middle path. Cut back anything near the house or along the main path, where tidiness matters most to you, and leave the rest. You'll see the difference by January, and we suspect you'll leave a little more standing next year.

Every year, around the end of November, we get the same email from at least one client. It usually starts politely and ends with a question about whether we've forgotten to cut the borders back. We haven't. We've left them standing on purpose, and we'd like to explain why.

draft.title: We've moved into the old dairy
draft.excerpt: After six years above a bike shop in Hexham, the studio has a new home with a proper drawing table, a kettle that works and a garden of its own.
draft.body:
After six happy years in two rooms above a bike shop on Priestpopple, we've moved. Our new home is the old dairy at Low Fold Farm, about three miles outside Hexham, and we couldn't be more pleased with it.

It's a long, low stone building with thick walls, small windows and a stone-flagged floor that's very cold in winter and very welcome in August. It was used as a store for years, and the farm let us take it on with a long lease in return for doing it up. Which we have, slowly, mostly at weekends, with a great deal of help from friends who will now be getting a lot of free garden advice.

## What's here

- One big room for the studio, with space for all of us to work at the same long table
- A small meeting room, where we'll talk through plans with clients over tea
- A plan chest we've been carrying around since 2019 and finally have room for
- A proper sink for washing soil off boots, plant samples and, occasionally, people

## The garden

The best part is outside. There's a walled yard to the south, about the size of a tennis court, that the farm used for calf pens. We've started turning it into a trial garden. We'll grow the plants we specify most often, try out the ones we're less sure about, and test combinations before we put them into anyone else's garden.

It's also, if we're honest, somewhere to go and stand for ten minutes when a drawing isn't working. Every design studio should have one.

## Come and see us

We'd love visitors. If you're a client, or thinking about becoming one, the kettle's always on and we're usually in from nine until half five, Monday to Friday. Do ring first, though, as we're often out on site, and the track down from the road is easier to find with directions.

Our new address is on the contact page. Our phone number and email haven't changed. And yes, there are still cows in the next field, so please shut the gate.

examples.title: Planting tulips and alliums in October
examples.excerpt: Two kinds of bulb, one month and a handful of grit. When to plant, how deep, how far apart, and what to do when they come up in March.
examples.body:
Every April, someone looks at our tulips and tells us they meant to plant some this year. What they meant was October. If you're reading this in October, you've still got time.

## Why October

Bulbs want soil that's cooling down but still workable. In the north, October is when those two overlap: the ground has lost its summer warmth, but it isn't yet cold and sodden, and a trowel still goes in without a fight.

Alliums are the early ones. They're happy to go in from September into October, and the sooner they're in, the sooner they get their roots down.

Tulips are better a little later. Wait until the weather has properly turned, towards the end of the month. Planting into colder soil helps you avoid tulip fire, a fungal disease that spots and twists the leaves and can spoil a whole planting. There's no prize for getting tulips in early. There's quite a big one for getting them in at all.

## How deep, how far apart

Two rules of thumb cover nearly everything. Write them on the back of an envelope and keep it at the potting bench.

- Depth: two to three times the height of the bulb
- Pointy end up (if you really can't tell, lay it on its side and it'll sort itself out)
- Tulips a bit deeper in pots and exposed spots, where the wind rocks tall stems
- Spacing in borders: about two bulb-widths apart
- Spacing in pots: closer, for a fuller look

If you're unsure, go deeper rather than shallower. A deep bulb stands steadier when a cold April wind comes through.

## Pots or borders

Both work. They just ask different things of you.

Pots are mostly about water, and getting rid of it. Make sure there are proper drainage holes, use a gritty compost (or mix a good amount of grit into your usual one), and stand the pots somewhere sheltered from the worst of the winter rain. Lifting them onto pot feet or a couple of bricks stops them sitting in a puddle. A pot that waterlogs in January is a pot of rotten bulbs by March.

Tulips in pots are easiest treated as annuals. Enjoy them, compost them when they're over and start again next autumn. Plenty of tulips dwindle after their first year anyway, so if yours come back, call it a bonus.

examples.title: Replanting a community orchard in Hebden Bridge
examples.excerpt: Forty-two fruit trees, three planting days, a lot of volunteers and quite a lot of cake. A different kind of project for us, and one of our favourites.
examples.body:
Most of our work is for private gardens. Every so often, though, something different comes along, and this was one of those. A residents' group in Hebden Bridge had taken on a steep, neglected field above the town with a handful of old apple trees in it, and they wanted to turn it back into an orchard everyone could use.

They had enthusiasm, a small grant and a great many volunteers. What they didn't have was a plan. That's where we came in.

## Starting with the old trees

There were eleven old trees on the site, mostly apples, a couple of damsons and one very large perry pear that nobody could identify. We had them looked at by a fruit specialist from the Northern Fruit Group, who confirmed that several were old local varieties worth keeping. Two were too far gone and came down. The rest were given a careful restorative prune, spread over three winters so as not to shock them.

## Choosing what to plant

We added forty-two new trees, chosen for three things: they had to be hardy enough for a cold Pennine hillside, they had to be varieties with some link to the north of England, and they had to fruit over a long season so there was always something to pick.

- Apples including 'Ribston Pippin', 'Keswick Codlin', 'Yorkshire Greening' and 'Lord Lambourne'
- Pears 'Hessle' and 'Catillac', both tough and reliable
- Damsons and plums, including 'Shropshire Prune' and 'Victoria'
- A few cobnuts along the top hedge, for the squirrels if nobody else

All of them are on vigorous rootstocks. On an exposed site, they need the strength, and a community orchard benefits from big trees you can stand under.

## The planting days

We ran three planting days in February, each with around thirty volunteers. We gave a short demonstration at the start, then split everyone into small groups, each with someone who had planted a tree before. By the end of the third day every tree was in, staked and guarded against rabbits and deer.

> Someone's grandchild planted the last tree. That felt right.

## The meadow underneath

Between the trees, we've started turning the grass into a wildflower meadow, sown with yellow rattle to weaken the grass, and mown into paths so people can walk through. It'll take a few years to come good. Orchards and meadows both reward patience.

## What happens next

The group now runs pruning workshops each winter and an apple day every October. We still go up a few times a year to see how things are getting on. The first proper crop is perhaps three years away, and we've already been promised a bottle of the perry.

data.title: We've moved into the old dairy
data.excerpt: After six years above a bike shop in Hexham, the studio has a new home with a proper drawing table, a kettle that works and a garden of its own.

content.text: After six happy years in two rooms above a bike shop on Priestpopple, we've moved. Our new home is the old dairy at Low Fold Farm, about three miles outside Hexham, and we couldn't be more pleased with it.

It's a long, low stone building with thick walls, small windows and a stone-flagged floor that's very cold in winter and very welcome in August. It was used as a store for years, and the farm let us take it on with a long lease in return for doing it up. Which we have, slowly, mostly at weekends, with a great deal of help from friends who will now be getting a lot of free garden advice.
What's here
One big room for the studio, with space for all of us to work at the same long table
A small meeting room, where we'll talk through plans with clients over tea
A plan chest we've been carrying around since 2019 and finally have room for
A proper sink for washing soil off boots, plant samples and, occasionally, people
The garden

The best part is outside. There's a walled yard to the south, about the size of a tennis court, that the farm used for calf pens. We've started turning it into a trial garden. We'll grow the plants we specify most often, try out the ones we're less sure about, and test combinations before we put them into anyone else's garden.
It's also, if we're honest, somewhere to go and stand for ten minutes when a drawing isn't working. Every design studio should have one.
Come and see us

We'd love visitors. If you're a client, or thinking about becoming one, the kettle's always on and we're usually in from nine until half five, Monday to Friday. Do ring first, though, as we're often out on site, and the track down from the road is easier to find with directions.
Our new address is on the contact page. Our phone number and email haven't changed. And yes, there are still cows in the next field, so please shut the gate.

draft.title: How a planting plan comes together
draft.excerpt: People often ask what they're actually paying for when they commission a planting plan. Here's what happens between the first visit and the drawing that arrives in the post.
draft.body:
A planting plan is the drawing that tells you, or whoever is doing the planting, exactly which plant goes where, and how many of each. It looks simple on paper. Getting to it takes a bit longer, and we think it's worth explaining what happens in between.

## We look at what's there

The first visit is mostly looking and asking. We dig a few holes to see what the soil is like. We note which way the garden faces, where the shade falls at different times of day, where water collects after rain and where it never does. We look at what's already growing well, both in your garden and in the gardens next door, because that tells us more than any soil test.

We also ask a lot of questions about you. How much time do you want to spend gardening? Do you want flowers to cut? Are there colours you love, or can't stand? Is there a dog who digs?

## We work out a palette

Back at the studio, we put together a plant palette: a long list of plants that will suit the conditions and the brief. Then we cut it down. And down again. A good planting usually has fewer kinds of plant than people expect, repeated across the space, so it holds together and reads as a whole.

At this stage we'll usually send over a page of images and a short note, so you can tell us if anything feels wrong before we go further.

## We draw it

The plan itself is drawn to scale, usually at 1:50. Each plant is shown at roughly the size it will be after three or four years, not the size it'll be when it arrives. That's why a freshly planted border looks a bit sparse. It's meant to.

We think about:

1. Structure first: the trees, shrubs and evergreens that give the garden its shape in winter
2. Then the main perennials and grasses, planted in drifts and repeated
3. Then the bulbs and smaller things that fill gaps and extend the season

## We hand it over properly

Along with the drawing, you get a plant schedule with quantities, pot sizes and suppliers, and a short care note for the first couple of years. If we're not doing the planting ourselves, we're happy to come back on the day and set the plants out in their pots, so whoever is planting can see the plan made real before a spade goes in.

> The drawing is the easy bit. The thinking behind it is what you're really paying for.

If you're weighing up whether a plan is worth it, our answer is that the cost is usually saved in plants that don't die and don't have to be moved twice.

examples.excerpt: Two kinds of bulb, one month and a handful of grit. When to plant, how deep, how far apart, and what to do when they come up in March.

## Why October

Bulbs want soil that's cooling down but still workable. In the north, October is when those two overlap: the ground has lost its summer warmth, but it isn't yet cold and sodden, and a trowel still goes in without a fight.

Alliums are the early ones. They're happy to go in from September into October, and the sooner they're in, the sooner they get their roots down.

Tulips are better a little later. Wait until the weather has properly turned, towards the end of the month. Planting into colder soil helps you avoid tulip fire, a fungal disease that spots and twists the leaves and can spoil a whole planting. There's no prize for getting tulips in early. There's quite a big one for getting them in at all.

## How deep, how far apart

Two rules of thumb cover nearly everything. Write them on the back of an envelope and keep it at the potting bench.

- Depth: two to three times the height of the bulb
- Pointy end up (if you really can't tell, lay it on its side and it'll sort itself out)
- Tulips a bit deeper in pots and exposed spots, where the wind rocks tall stems
- Spacing in borders: about two bulb-widths apart
- Spacing in pots: closer, for a fuller look

If you're unsure, go deeper rather than shallower. A deep bulb stands steadier when a cold April wind comes through.

draft.title: Ten jobs for the first warm weekend
draft.excerpt: When the sun finally comes out and you want to be outside, here's where to put your energy so the rest of the year goes more easily.
draft.body:
It happens every year. After weeks of grey, there's a Saturday when the sun comes out, the air feels soft, and everyone in the country heads into the garden at once. It's a good feeling. It also tends to lead to a lot of enthusiastic digging in the wrong places.

So here's our list. Ten jobs that pay you back for the rest of the year, roughly in the order we'd do them.

## Before anything else

1. **Cut back the old growth.** If you left your borders standing over winter (and we hope you did), now is the time. Cut grasses and perennials down to just above the new shoots. Chop the stems and compost them.
2. **Weed while the weeds are small.** An hour now saves a day in June. Get the perennial weeds out by the root, especially couch grass and creeping buttercup.
3. **Mulch.** Once the soil is weeded and damp, put down five centimetres of compost or well-rotted manure over every bare bit. It holds moisture, feeds the soil and keeps the next lot of weeds down. Of everything on this list, this is the one we'd never skip.

## Then the plants

4. **Divide summer-flowering perennials** that have got too big, if you didn't get to it in autumn.
5. **Feed shrubs and roses** with a general fertiliser, and give the roses a light prune if they need it.
6. **Plant summer-flowering bulbs** such as *Gladiolus murielae*, lilies and *Eucomis*, in pots or the border.
7. **Sow hardy annuals** directly where they're to flower. Cornflowers, *Nigella* and calendula are almost foolproof.

## And the rest

8. **Give the lawn its first cut,** with the blades high. Don't scalp it. It's been through a lot.
9. **Check ties and stakes** on young trees. Loosen anything cutting into the bark.
10. **Clean the greenhouse glass,** inside and out. Seedlings need every scrap of light they can get this early in the year.

## What not to do

Don't rush tender plants out. A warm weekend in March is nearly always followed by a frost, and in the north we wouldn't put dahlias or tomatoes out until the end of May. Don't dig wet soil either. If it sticks to your boots, leave it a few more days, or you'll squash the structure out of it.

> The garden is never as far behind as it feels in March.

And don't try to do all ten in one go. Pick two or three, do them well, and then sit in the sun with a cup of tea. That counts as gardening too.

examples.title: Planting tulips and alliums in October
examples.excerpt: Two kinds of bulb, one month and a handful of grit. When to plant, how deep, how far apart, and what to do when they come up in March.
examples.body:
Every April, someone looks at our tulips and tells us they meant to plant some this year. What they meant was October. If you're reading this in October, you've still got time.

## Why October

Bulbs want soil that's cooling down but still workable. In the north, October is when those two overlap: the ground has lost its summer warmth, but it isn't yet cold and sodden, and a trowel still goes in without a fight.

Alliums are the early ones. They're happy to go in from September into October, and the sooner they're in, the sooner they get their roots down.

Tulips are better a little later. Wait until the weather has properly turned, towards the end of the month. Planting into colder soil helps you avoid tulip fire, a fungal disease that spots and twists the leaves and can spoil a whole planting. There's no prize for getting tulips in early. There's quite a big one for getting them in at all.

## How deep, how far apart

Two rules of thumb cover nearly everything. Write them on the back of an envelope and keep it at the potting bench.

- Depth: two to three times the height of the bulb
- Pointy end up (if you really can't tell, lay it on its side and it'll sort itself out)
- Tulips a bit deeper in pots and exposed spots, where the wind rocks tall stems
- Spacing in borders: about two bulb-widths apart
- Spacing in pots: closer, for a fuller look

If you're unsure, go deeper rather than shallower. A deep bulb stands steadier when a cold April wind comes through.

## Pots or borders

Both work. They just ask different things of you.

Pots are mostly about water, and getting rid of it. Make sure there are proper drainage holes, use a gritty compost (or mix a good amount of grit into your usual one), and stand the pots somewhere sheltered from the worst of the winter rain. Lifting them onto pot feet or a couple of bricks stops them sitting in a puddle. A pot that waterlogs in January is a pot of rotten bulbs by March.

Tulips in pots are easiest treated as annuals. Enjoy them, compost them when they're over and start again next autumn. Plenty of tulips dwindle after their first year anyway, so if yours come back, call it a bonus.

In borders, plant in drifts or groups, not single lines. A row of tulips along a path looks like a queue. Dig a wide hole, set a group of bulbs in it, then do the same again a little way off, with uneven gaps between. It looks far more like they meant to be there.

Then mark where they are. A short cane or a label is enough. By July the leaves will have gone and you'll have forgotten, and a spade through a clump of bulbs is a sad way to remember.

Alliums are happy to stay in a border for years. Allium 'Purple Sensation' earns its keep twice: once in flower in late spring, and again when the seedheads stand on through summer.

## A lesson from Corbridge

In the walled garden we've been bringing back near Corbridge, we planted Tulipa 'Ballerina' and Tulipa 'Queen of Night' in the borders in the last week of October, with Allium 'Purple Sensation' between them. Then November was wet. The ground there is heavy clay, and about a third of the tulips rotted. Every single allium came up.

The next autumn we put a handful of grit under each tulip bulb. We lost almost none. If your soil is clay, this is the one step we'd never skip.

## What to do in March

March is when you find out how October went. A few things are worth doing:

- Check pots haven't dried out, or gone the other way and waterlogged
- Watch for shoots coming through, and for slugs, which are very fond of young tulip leaves
- Feed if they look like they need it, especially anything you're hoping to keep for another year
- Note the gaps while you can see them, for next autumn's order

That last one is the job everyone skips. Take a few photos in April when everything's out. In October you won't remember where the bare patch was, and the photos will.

## The short version

- Alliums in now, tulips towards the end of the month
- Two to three times the bulb's height, pointy end up
- Grit in the pots, and under the bulbs on clay
- Drifts, not lines
- A cane where every group went

For the rest of this month's jobs, our piece on what to do in the garden in October has the list. When the weather finally turns, Ten jobs for the first warm weekend picks up where March leaves off.

A spring garden is mostly planted in autumn.

So go and buy some bulbs this month and get them in. And if you'd like a hand with a planting plan for the whole garden, not just the bulbs, it might be worth a conversation.

And if October gets away from you (it usually does), don't leave the tulips in the shed. They'll still go in through November, and often into December, as long as the ground isn't frozen. They may flower a little late. They'll still flower.

examples.title: Replanting a community orchard in Hebden Bridge
examples.excerpt: Forty-two fruit trees, three planting days, a lot of volunteers and quite a lot of cake. A different kind of project for us, and one of our favourites.
examples.body:
Most of our work is for private gardens. Every so often, though, something different comes along, and this was one of those. A residents' group in Hebden Bridge had taken on a steep, neglected field above the town with a handful of old apple trees in it, and they wanted to turn it back into an orchard everyone could use.

They had enthusiasm, a small grant and a great many volunteers. What they didn't have was a plan. That's where we came in.

## Starting with the old trees

There were eleven old trees on the site, mostly apples, a couple of damsons and one very large perry pear that nobody could identify. We had them looked at by a fruit specialist from the Northern Fruit Group, who confirmed that several were old local varieties worth keeping. Two were too far gone and came down. The rest were given a careful restorative prune, spread over three winters so as not to shock them.

## Choosing what to plant

We added forty-two new trees, chosen for three things: they had to be hardy enough for a cold Pennine hillside, they had to be varieties with some link to the north of England, and they had to fruit over a long season so there was always something to pick.

- Apples including 'Ribston Pippin', 'Keswick Codlin', 'Yorkshire Greening' and 'Lord Lambourne'
- Pears 'Hessle' and 'Catillac', both tough and reliable
- Damsons and plums, including 'Shropshire Prune' and 'Victoria'
- A few cobnuts along the top hedge, for the squirrels if nobody else

All of them are on vigorous rootstocks. On an exposed site, they need the strength, and a community orchard benefits from big trees you can stand under.

## The planting days

We ran three planting days in February, each with around thirty volunteers. We gave a short demonstration at the start, then split everyone into small groups, each with someone who had planted a tree before. By the end of the third day every tree was in, staked and guarded against rabbits and deer.

> Someone's grandchild planted the last tree. That felt right.

## The meadow underneath

Between the trees, we've started turning the grass into a wildflower meadow, sown with yellow rattle to weaken the grass, and mown into paths so people can walk through. It'll take a few years to come good. Orchards and meadows both reward patience.

## What happens next

The group now runs pruning workshops each winter and an apple day every October. We still go up a few times a year to see how things are getting on. The first proper crop is perhaps three years away, and we've already been promised a bottle of the perry.

It happens every year. After weeks of grey, there's a Saturday when the sun comes out, the air feels soft, and everyone in the country heads into the garden at once. It's a good feeling. It also tends to lead to a lot of enthusiastic digging in the wrong places.

So here's our list. Ten jobs that pay you back for the rest of the year, roughly in the order we'd do them.

## Before anything else

1. **Cut back the old growth.** If you left your borders standing over winter (and we hope you did), now is the time. Cut grasses and perennials down to just above the new shoots. Chop the stems and compost them.
2. **Weed while the weeds are small.** An hour now saves a day in June. Get the perennial weeds out by the root, especially couch grass and creeping buttercup.
3. **Mulch.** Once the soil is weeded and damp, put down five centimetres of compost or well-rotted manure over every bare bit. It holds moisture, feeds the soil and keeps the next lot of weeds down. Of everything on this list, this is the one we'd never skip.

## Then the plants

4. **Divide summer-flowering perennials** that have got too big, if you didn't get to it in autumn.
5. **Feed shrubs and roses** with a general fertiliser, and give the roses a light prune if they need it.
6. **Plant summer-flowering bulbs** such as *Gladiolus murielae*, lilies and *Eucomis*, in pots or the border.
7. **Sow hardy annuals** directly where they're to flower. Cornflowers, *Nigella* and calendula are almost foolproof.

draft.title: Priya joins the studio
draft.excerpt: We're delighted to welcome Priya Sandhu as a garden designer, bringing a background in ecology and a very good eye for grasses.
draft.body:
We're very pleased to say that Priya Sandhu has joined the studio as a garden designer. Many of you will already have met her, as she's been helping us on a few projects over the past year while finishing her diploma. Now she's here properly, with a desk, a key to the old dairy and her own mug.

## A bit about Priya

Priya grew up in Wolverhampton and came to gardens by a slightly roundabout route. She studied ecology at Newcastle, then spent five years with a wildlife trust, surveying grasslands and wetlands across the North Pennines. It was there, she says, that she started noticing how good the plants looked together, not just how rare they were.

That led to a garden design diploma, a lot of evening classes and, eventually, to us. She brings a way of thinking about plants as communities rather than individuals, which suits the way we work very well, and a knowledge of native flora that has already won a couple of arguments in the studio.

## What she'll be working on

Priya will be leading on some of our larger rural projects, especially where there's a habitat or biodiversity side to the brief. She's already deep into a plan for a former quarry near Allendale, which we'll write about once it's in the ground. She'll also be looking after our trial garden at the dairy, which means she gets to decide what lives and what goes on the compost heap.

## In her own words

We asked Priya what she was most looking forward to. She said:

> Seeing something I've drawn actually grow. Survey work is about recording what's there. This is about adding something, and then coming back in five years to see if I was right.

## Five quick questions

1. **Favourite plant?***Molinia caerulea* 'Transparent'. "It's there and then it isn't."
2. **Most overrated plant?** "I'm not saying. I'll have to work with it at some point."
3. **Best garden you've visited?** Scampston, in North Yorkshire.
4. **Tea or coffee?** Tea, very strong.
5. **Wellies or walking boots?** "Wellies. Always wellies."

Please do say hello if you see her on site or at the studio. She's the one with the hand lens.

examples.title: Planting tulips and alliums in October
examples.excerpt: Two kinds of bulb, one month and a handful of grit. When to plant, how deep, how far apart, and what to do when they come up in March.
examples.body:
Every April, someone looks at our tulips and tells us they meant to plant some this year. What they meant was October. If you're reading this in October, you've still got time.

## Why October

Bulbs want soil that's cooling down but still workable. In the north, October is when those two overlap: the ground has lost its summer warmth, but it isn't yet cold and sodden, and a trowel still goes in without a fight.

Alliums are the early ones. They're happy to go in from September into October, and the sooner they're in, the sooner they get their roots down.

Tulips are better a little later. Wait until the weather has properly turned, towards the end of the month. Planting into colder soil helps you avoid tulip fire, a fungal disease that spots and twists the leaves and can spoil a whole planting. There's no prize for getting tulips in early. There's quite a big one for getting them in at all.

## How deep, how far apart

Two rules of thumb cover nearly everything. Write them on the back of an envelope and keep it at the potting bench.

- Depth: two to three times the height of the bulb
- Pointy end up (if you really can't tell, lay it on its side and it'll sort itself out)
- Tulips a bit deeper in pots and exposed spots, where the wind rocks tall stems
- Spacing in borders: about two bulb-widths apart
- Spacing in pots: closer, for a fuller look

If you're unsure, go deeper rather than shallower. A deep bulb stands steadier when a cold April wind comes through.

## Pots or borders

Both work. They just ask different things of you.

Pots are mostly about water, and getting rid of it. Make sure there are proper drainage holes, use a gritty compost (or mix a good amount of grit into your usual one), and stand the pots somewhere sheltered from the worst of the winter rain. Lifting them onto pot feet or a couple of bricks stops them sitting in a puddle. A pot that waterlogs in January is a pot of rotten bulbs by March.

Tulips in pots are easiest treated as annuals. Enjoy them, compost them when they're over and start again next autumn. Plenty of tulips dwindle after their first year anyway, so if yours come back, call it a bonus.

In borders, plant in drifts or groups, not single lines. A row of tulips along a path looks like a queue. Dig a wide hole, set a group of bulbs in it, then do the same again a little way off, with uneven gaps between. It looks far more like they meant to be there.

Then mark where they are. A short cane or a label is enough. By July the leaves will have gone and you'll have forgotten, and a spade through a clump of bulbs is a sad way to remember.

Alliums are happy to stay in a border for years. Allium 'Purple Sensation' earns its keep twice: once in flower in late spring, and again when the seedheads stand on through summer.

## A lesson from Corbridge

In the walled garden we've been bringing back near Corbridge, we planted Tulipa 'Ballerina' and Tulipa 'Queen of Night' in the borders in the last week of October, with Allium 'Purple Sensation' between them. Then November was wet. The ground there is heavy clay, and about a third of the tulips rotted. Every single allium came up.

The next autumn we put a handful of grit under each tulip bulb. We lost almost none. If your soil is clay, this is the one step we'd never skip.

## What to do in March

March is when you find out how October went. A few things are worth doing:

- Check pots haven't dried out, or gone the other way and waterlogged
- Watch for shoots coming through, and for slugs, which are very fond of young tulip leaves
- Feed if they look like they need it, especially anything you're hoping to keep for another year
- Note the gaps while you can see them, for next autumn's order

That last one is the job everyone skips. Take a few photos in April when everything's out. In October you won't remember where the bare patch was, and the photos will.

## The short version

- Alliums in now, tulips towards the end of the month
- Two to three times the bulb's height, pointy end up
- Grit in the pots, and under the bulbs on clay
- Drifts, not lines
- A cane where every group went

For the rest of this month's jobs, our piece on what to do in the garden in October has the list. When the weather finally turns, Ten jobs for the first warm weekend picks up where March leaves off.

A spring garden is mostly planted in autumn.

So go and buy some bulbs this month and get them in. And if you'd like a hand with a planting plan for the whole garden, not just the bulbs, it might be worth a conversation.

And if October gets away from you (it usually does), don't leave the tulips in the shed. They'll still go in through November, and often into December, as long as the ground isn't frozen. They may flower a little late. They'll still flower.

examples.title: Replanting a community orchard in Hebden Bridge
examples.excerpt: Forty-two fruit trees, three planting days, a lot of volunteers and quite a lot of cake. A different kind of project for us, and one of our favourites.
examples.body:
Most of our work is for private gardens. Every so often, though, something different comes along, and this was one of those. A residents' group in Hebden Bridge had taken on a steep, neglected field above the town with a handful of old apple trees in it, and they wanted to turn it back into an orchard everyone could use.

They had enthusiasm, a small grant and a great many volunteers. What they didn't have was a plan. That's where we came in.

## Starting with the old trees

There were eleven old trees on the site, mostly apples, a couple of damsons and one very large perry pear that nobody could identify. We had them looked at by a fruit specialist from the Northern Fruit Group, who confirmed that several were old local varieties worth keeping. Two were too far gone and came down. The rest were given a careful restorative prune, spread over three winters so as not to shock them.

## Choosing what to plant

We added forty-two new trees, chosen for three things: they had to be hardy enough for a cold Pennine hillside, they had to be varieties with some link to the north of England, and they had to fruit over a long season so there was always something to pick.

- Apples including 'Ribston Pippin', 'Keswick Codlin', 'Yorkshire Greening' and 'Lord Lambourne'
- Pears 'Hessle' and 'Catillac', both tough and reliable
- Damsons and plums, including 'Shropshire Prune' and 'Victoria'
- A few cobnuts along the top hedge, for the squirrels if nobody else

All of them are on vigorous rootstocks. On an exposed site, they need the strength, and a community orchard benefits from big trees you can stand under.

## The planting days

We ran three planting days in February, each with around thirty volunteers. We gave a short demonstration at the start, then split everyone into small groups, each with someone who had planted a tree before. By the end of the third day every tree was in, staked and guarded against rabbits and deer.

> Someone's grandchild planted the last tree. That felt right.

## The meadow underneath

Between the trees, we've started turning the grass into a wildflower meadow, sown with yellow rattle to weaken the grass, and mown into paths so people can walk through. It'll take a few years to come good. Orchards and meadows both reward patience.

## What happens next

The group now runs pruning workshops each winter and an apple day every October. We still go up a few times a year to see how things are getting on. The first proper crop is perhaps three years away, and we've already been promised a bottle of the perry.
